summary: Defines an alternative way to exchange incident and indicator information, using a JSON data model encoded in JSON or CBOR. It gives the same information as the XML Incident Object Description Exchange Format in RFC 7970.

eli5.summary: Security teams share notes about problems. This lets them use a lighter, more modern note format instead of XML.

questions: how to encode iodef in cbor
subtitle: A JSON and CBOR version of the IODEF security-incident data model, carrying the same information as the XML original.

tldr.problem: IODEF, the standard format for exchanging security incident reports and indicators, was only defined as XML, while many tools and automation pipelines prefer JSON or compact binary formats.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC maps the IODEF information model onto JSON data types, defines the data model in CDDL (with a JSON Schema as an informative appendix), and gives integer map keys so the same model can be encoded compactly in CBOR.
tldr.outcome: IODEF JSON provides all of the expressivity of IODEF XML, so implementers and operators get an alternative format for exchanging the same information.

today: RFC 8727 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It gives the JSON and CBOR form of the model defined in RFC 7970.

sections.title: Why a JSON Binding of IODEF
sections.content:
The Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF, RFC 7970) defines a representation for security incident reports and indicators that operational security teams commonly exchange. It has a UML information model and a corresponding XML schema data model. This RFC calls these IODEF UML and IODEF XML.

To help automate incident response, the authors argue that IODEF documents and implementations should also support the JSON format (RFC 8259) and its encoding in CBOR (RFC 7049). This document therefore defines an alternate implementation of the same UML information model, called IODEF JSON, by specifying a JSON data model in the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL, RFC 8610) and a JSON Schema.

The normative data model is the CDDL in Section 6. Sections 2 and 3 describe its data types and elements, and Section 4 gives examples.
sections.eli5: There was already a way to write down a computer-security problem report using one style of writing. This RFC says how to write the very same report in two other styles that many programs like better.

sections.title: Data Types in JSON and CBOR
sections.content:
IODEF JSON implements the abstract data types of RFC 7970, Section 2. Table 1 of the RFC maps each to a JSON type and Table 2 maps each to a CBOR type and CDDL prelude type. For example, INTEGER, REAL, STRING, DATETIME and URL map to a JSON integer, number or string, and in CBOR to an integer, a float32, text, a tagged date-time (tag 0) and a URI (tag 32). BYTE and HEXBIN map to JSON strings and to CBOR tags 22 and 23.

Several types are complex. A multilingual string (ML_STRING) is an object with value, lang and translation-id, or simply a text string. SOFTWARE is an object with SoftwareReference, URL and Description. STRUCTUREDINFO, the structure first specified in RFC 7203, is an object with SpecID, ext-SpecID, ContentID, RawData and Reference. EXTENSION is the generic way to add information not otherwise represented in IODEF.

When raw data is embedded, base64 encoding (RFC 4648, Section 4) MUST be used for JSON IODEF, while binary representation MUST be used for CBOR IODEF.
sections.eli5: Each kind of thing in the report, such as a date, a web address or a number, has a matching way to write it in JSON and in the compact binary form. Fancy things, like text in several languages, become small labeled boxes.

sections.title: Differences from IODEF XML
sections.content:
The model has the same classes as IODEF XML, such as IODEF-Document, Incident and Indicator, with the same elements and attributes. Section 3.2 lists how the JSON form differs, so that documents can be converted in both directions.

  • Attributes and elements of a class are all JSON attributes, and the order in which they appear is ignored.
  • The Flow, ApplicationHeader, SignatureData, IndicatorData, ObservableReference and Record wrapper classes are deleted. The classes that held them now directly contain the instances that used to sit inside them.
  • An ML_STRING element may be a plain string or an object. Implementations need to parse both forms. When a plain string is used, parsers can assume its language is en. Converting between XML and JSON must preserve the information in the original data.
  • The extension classes from RFC 7203 are represented by the STRUCTUREDINFO class.
  • Signature, X509Data and RawData are base64 in JSON and binary in CBOR. XML IODEF used HEXBIN because XML cannot embed binaries directly.
  • The ipv6-net-mask attribute stays available for backward compatibility, but its use is not recommended.
  • ENUM values are extensible and managed by IANA, and the same values serve both RFC 7970 implementations and the JSON and CBOR bindings.

JSON numbers have full precision only for integers between -2^53 and 2^53, so values outside that range need care.
sections.eli5: Turning the old report style into the new one is like moving house. Most things go straight across, a few extra boxes get unpacked, and the RFC lists exactly which ones so nothing gets lost.

sections.title: Examples: A Minimal Document and a Campaign
sections.content:
Section 4.1 shows a document with only the mandatory elements, in both JSON and CBOR. It has version 2.0, lang en, and one Incident with a purpose of reporting, a restriction of private, an IncidentID, a GenerationTime and a Contact with an email address.

Section 4.2 shows indicators from a campaign: a watch-purpose incident that names a threat actor and a campaign in RelatedActivity, gives a description and an impact assessment, and lists command-and-control domain indicators. The RFC states that these examples do not represent the full capabilities of the data model or the only way to encode particular information.
sections.eli5: The examples show the shortest possible report, with just the must-have parts, and then a bigger one about a made-up group of bad actors and the tricks they use.

sections.title: Mapkeys for Compact CBOR
sections.content:
To keep CBOR messages small, Section 5 assigns every JSON key name an integer mapkey (a cborkey), so CBOR maps use numbers instead of text names. The names are prefixed with iodef-. The assignments run from iodef-version = -24 and iodef-lang = -23, through iodef-Incident = -19 and iodef-purpose = -2, to iodef-status = 0 and iodef-IncidentID = 2, and onwards.

The minimal example in Section 4.1 shows the effect. Its CBOR form is a map whose first key is the negative integer -24 (the version), followed by the text 2.0.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing the full name on every drawer, the compact form numbers the drawers. A short number takes far less room than a long name.

sections.title: The CDDL Data Model and JSON Schema
sections.content:
Section 6 is the normative IODEF data model, written in CDDL. The mapkeys come first for readability, followed by definitions of each class, with optional members marked ? and repeated members as [+ ...] arrays. Appendix A explains how the CDDL prelude types such as text, tdate, uri and float32 map onto JSON.

Appendix B gives a JSON Schema for the same data model. It is informative only, so the CDDL is the definition to follow.
sections.eli5: The RFC contains the official rulebook for what a report may contain, written in a special rule-writing language. A second rulebook in another language is included just as a helper.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document maps XML IODEF to JSON and adds no security considerations beyond those of RFC 7970. It does point out that the conversion issues in Section 3.2 can arise when converting between XML IODEF and JSON IODEF, and says implementers should be aware of them to avoid unintended outcomes. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is risky here, but when you translate a report from one style to the other, be careful not to drop or change anything by accident.
